title: Shunt infection (S. epidermidis): biofilm (extracellular polysaccharide matrix)
vignette: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of high fever, irritability, and photophobia. He recently underwent ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement for congenital hydrocephalus. On physical examination, his temperature is 38.3 C (101 F), and passive flexion of the neck results in spontaneous flexion of the hips and knees. Blood cultures grow coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. Which of the following is the most important virulence mechanism by which this bacterium causes disease?

clues.note: A prosthetic device (VP shunt) is a foreign body that Staphylococcus epidermidis colonizes - the setup for a device-associated infection.

clues.text: passive flexion of the neck results in spontaneous flexion of the hips and knees
clues.note: This is a positive Brudzinski sign, indicating meningitis (here, shunt-associated).
Coagulase-NEGATIVE Staphylococcus = Staphylococcus epidermidis, the leading cause of prosthetic-device infections via biofilm formation.

whatMatters: A device (VP shunt) infection with COAGULASE-NEGATIVE Staphylococcus = Staphylococcus epidermidis. Its key virulence mechanism is forming a BIOFILM - synthesizing an EXTRACELLULAR POLYSACCHARIDE MATRIX that adheres to foreign material and shields it from antibiotics and host defenses. Answer E.
strategy: Link foreign-body infection + coagulase-negative Staph to S. epidermidis and its signature: biofilm (extracellular polysaccharide/glycocalyx matrix). Reject intracellular existence (Listeria/Salmonella/mycobacteria), polysaccharide CAPSULE (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis), protein A (S. aureus - binds Fc, not S. epidermidis's main mechanism), and exotoxins (S. aureus toxins), none of which is the S. epidermidis device mechanism.

options.text: Presence of protein A on the cell wall
Synthesis of an extracellular polysaccharide matrix

eliminations.label: Intracellular existence - facultative/obligate intracellular organisms
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: surviving inside host cells (e.g., Listeria, Salmonella, Mycobacterium, Rickettsia). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: S. epidermidis is an extracellular biofilm-former, not an intracellular pathogen. ✅ Correct if: an intracellular organism.

eliminations.label: Outer polysaccharide capsule - encapsulated bacteria
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an antiphagocytic capsule (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, N. meningitidis). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: S. epidermidis's device virulence is the BIOFILM matrix, not a classic antiphagocytic capsule. ✅ Correct if: an encapsulated organism dangerous in asplenia.

eliminations.label: Protein A - Staphylococcus aureus
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: protein A on S. AUREUS binds the Fc region of IgG to inhibit opsonization/phagocytosis. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that's an S. aureus (coagulase-POSITIVE) virulence factor; this is coagulase-negative S. epidermidis. ✅ Correct if: S. aureus immune evasion.

eliminations.label: Release of exotoxins - S. aureus toxins
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: exotoxins (e.g., staphylococcal enterotoxins, TSST-1, exfoliative toxin) are S. aureus products. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: exotoxin production is not the mechanism of S. epidermidis device infection. ✅ Correct if: toxin-mediated S. aureus disease (food poisoning, TSS).

reasoning: VP shunt (foreign body) infection with coagulase-negative Staphylococcus = Staphylococcus epidermidis
S. epidermidis adheres to prosthetic material and multiplies within a self-made matrix
This biofilm is an extracellular polysaccharide matrix that resists antibiotics and immune clearance
-> synthesis of an extracellular polysaccharide matrix; answer E
mechanism: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-NEGATIVE, catalase-positive component of normal skin flora and the most common cause of infections associated with FOREIGN BODIES (prosthetic valves, catheters, and ventriculoperitoneal shunts). Its defining virulence mechanism is BIOFILM formation: after adhering to device surfaces (coated with host proteins like fibrinogen/fibronectin), the bacteria proliferate and secrete an EXTRACELLULAR POLYSACCHARIDE MATRIX (glycocalyx/slime) that encases the colony. This biofilm acts as a barrier to antibiotic penetration and impairs host defenses (opsonization, neutrophil migration), so device-associated infections are persistent and often require REMOVAL of the hardware. In this child, the shunt seeded a biofilm-associated meningitis (positive Brudzinski sign). The distractors are virulence mechanisms of other organisms: intracellular survival (Listeria/Salmonella/mycobacteria), antiphagocytic capsule (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis), and protein A/exotoxins (S. aureus, coagulase-positive).

difficulty.text: First Aid Micro > S. epidermidis: coagulase-negative, biofilm on prosthetic devices (extracellular polysaccharide matrix); infects shunts/catheters/valves; often requires device removal.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Foreign-body infection + coagulase-negative Staph = S. epidermidis biofilm (extracellular polysaccharide matrix).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on biofilm, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, glycocalyx, capsule vs biofilm, or Brudzinski sign? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Capsule = encapsulated bacteria; protein A + exotoxins = S. aureus; intracellular existence = other pathogens - not S. epidermidis's device mechanism.
